base.title: 1 · An atom that changes
base.body: A radionuclide has an unstable nucleus that can transform and release particles or radiation. Observe the clues and ask yes/no questions.

base.title: 2 · Colours as clues
base.body: Yellow represents alpha, blue beta-minus, and orange positrons or electron capture. Colours simplify the main branches; weak branches may appear only in the scientific record.

base.title: 3 · From everyday life to space
base.body: Medicine, nature, homes, food, industry and space are broad categories. Start with broad questions, then ask about specific applications when few cards remain.

base.title: 4 · Half-life
base.body: After one half-life, about half the original radioactive nuclei remain. Eight becomes four, then two: these are expected numbers; individual decays are random. Activity is measured in becquerels (Bq).

base.title: 5 · Memorable stories
base.body: Radon in homes, potassium-40 in the body, carbon-14 dating and medical imaging provide memorable clues. The game tests the documented associations on its cards.

intermediate.title: 1 · Protons and neutrons
intermediate.body: Protons determine the element. Isotopes share the same proton number but have different neutron numbers. Ask whether there are more than twenty protons or thirty neutrons.

intermediate.title: 2 · Z, A and N
intermediate.body: Z is the proton number, A the mass number and N = A − Z the neutron number. Each card describes a particular radionuclide, not just its chemical element.

intermediate.title: 3 · Alpha, beta and gamma
intermediate.body: Alpha particles usually have a short range. Beta radiation consists of electrons or positrons. Gamma rays are photons. Penetration depends on energy and the material traversed.

intermediate.title: 4 · Time scales
intermediate.body: Ask about seconds, minutes, hours, days, months or years, or use a numeric comparison. Intermediate and expert games allow two time questions per player. Displayed values are rounded; comparisons use full stored seconds.

intermediate.title: 5 · From everyday life to space
intermediate.body: Medicine, nature, homes, food, industry and space are broad categories. Start with broad questions, then ask about specific applications when few cards remain.

expert.title: 1 · Expert questions
expert.body: Explore Z/A/N, chemical families, physical state, melting point, decay modes and nuclear applications. Missing numerical data are never replaced by zero. Check the proposed interpretation before confirming.

expert.title: 2 · Half-life and mean life
expert.body: For exponential decay, N(t) = N₀ exp(−λt), T½ = ln 2 / λ and mean life τ = 1 / λ = T½ / ln 2. Both half-life and mean-life questions use the shared time-question allowance.

expert.title: 3 · Neutron capture
expert.body: Cross section is measured in barns and depends on the target, reaction and neutron energy. Capture (n,γ) differs from total absorption. The five inherited numerical values refer to thermal neutrons at 2200 m/s.

intermediate.body: Chemical family, state and melting point describe the element. Decay and half-life describe the radionuclide. Distinguish alkali metals from alkaline earth metals, and transition from post-transition metals.

expert.title: 4 · NGATLAS data
expert.body: NGATLAS reports capture cross sections versus energy. This release preserves five values from the earlier game. The wider import was not validated and remains disabled. Missing data do not mean zero.

expert.title: 5 · Chains and relationships
expert.body: A radionuclide may be a fission product, a natural-chain member, a generator parent or daughter, or an activation product. These are different relationships.
